analysis.one_liner: Taxes hedge funds and other investor entities 50% on each new home they buy and forces them to sell off large single-family rental portfolios, funding down-payment grants.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote after being referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new federal tax aimed at hedge funds and similar pooled-money investors that buy up single-family homes to rent out. Entities managing $50 million or more would pay a tax equal to 50% of the price of every home they acquire after the law takes effect, and would have to gradually sell down existing holdings—dropping to zero for hedge funds over nine years. Money raised would go into a new trust fund for grants to state agencies that help families cover down payments, with priority for buyers of homes sold off by the taxed investors. The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families trying to buy a first home would benefit twice: investor buying pressure on entry-level homes would shrink, and a wave of investor-owned homes would be sold off, with down-payment grant recipients given priority for those purchases. Renters in investor-owned neighborhoods could also gain if more homes shift to owner-occupancy, since investor-owned rentals are associated with higher rents and weaker maintenance in some markets.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a tax equal to 50% of fair market value on every single-family residence newly acquired by a covered investor entity after enactment, directly raising the cost of further investor purchases [S3].

Requires covered investors to shrink their existing single-family holdings over nine years, down to zero for hedge fund taxpayers ($50 million or more in assets) and to 50 homes for other covered entities, with a $50,000-per-home annual tax on holdings above the limit [S3].

Creates a Housing Downpayment Trust Fund funded by the new tax, paying for grants to state housing finance agencies for down-payment assistance to homebuyers, with priority given to buyers of homes sold by the covered investors [S3].

Defines covered taxpayers to include partnerships, corporations, and REITs that pool investor money, and treats related companies as one owner to prevent splitting portfolios to dodge the limits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporate owners of single-family rental homes—hedge funds, private equity firms, and real estate investment trusts—would bear the cost: a 50% tax on new acquisitions, a growing annual tax on unsold holdings, and forced divestiture of rental portfolios. Their tenant-rental business model in the single-family sector would be substantially curtailed. Some of the cost could be passed to tenants through rents in the short run, though the bill is designed to push homes to owner-occupancy.

drawbacks.text: The bill targets pooled-money investors and single-family rentals, not all corporate owners, so large landlords structured outside those definitions could keep buying homes [S3].

Forcing rapid divestiture of hundreds of thousands of rental homes could disrupt tenants if homes are sold to buyers who occupy them or reprice rents during the transition, and a fire-sale of portfolios could temporarily destabilize local rental markets [S3].

A 50% acquisition tax raises investor costs but does not cap what owner-occupant buyers can pay, so in markets where investor demand cools, prices could still be set by other buyers; the tax also applies to homes of 1-to-4 units, which could sweep in small landlords using normal financing structures [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families priced out by investor competition, the benefits are direct and large: fewer investor buyers competing for starter homes, a mandated sell-off of investor holdings, and dedicated down-payment help aimed first at those very homes. The main honest costs are transition risks for tenants in investor-owned homes and possible gaps where the definitions let some large landlords escape. The bill targets a specific and widely criticized practice, and its design—forcing divestiture rather than just taxing it—goes further than most proposals in this area.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Ways and Means and Financial Services committees on the day it was introduced and never advanced—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote—before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Smith introduced the bill on December 5, 2023, with Reps. Sanchez and Williams of Georgia as original cosponsors [S3].
The House referred it to both the Ways and Means Committee and the Financial Services Committee on the day of introduction [S1], [S5].
No further action was recorded for the remainder of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025 [S1], [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large investors in single-family rental homes—hedge funds, private equity, and REIT landlords—kept their acquisitions and rental income untouched, since no tax or divestiture requirement was ever enacted. First-time buyers gained nothing from the bill's proposed down-payment grants or forced sell-offs because the bill never advanced. Committee chairs with jurisdiction over tax and financial services legislation faced no pressure to act, and the issue was left to the next Congress to revisit or drop entirely.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate landlords and hedge fund investors

for.name: Rep. Adam Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 17 Democratic cosponsors; the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee lent his name to a tax-and-housing bill outside his committee portfolio.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee with primary jurisdiction over the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral, letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee with shared jurisdiction over housing and financial provisions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans controlling the House and its committees, the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Single-family rental investors (hedge funds, private equity, REIT landlords)
industries.note: A 50% tax on every new home bought, plus forced sell-down of existing portfolios over nine years, directly attacks the business model of large corporate single-family landlords. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against homebuyers who would face less investor competition and receive down-payment help funded by the tax.

industries.industry: First-time homebuyers and mortgage lenders serving them
industries.note: A new trust fund would pay for down-payment grants, increasing the pool of financed first-time buyers, with priority for homes divested by taxed investors.
